t: You have seen all the parts. Now build one that can stay alive.
You have met every part. Now put them together into something that survives.
Every component you have met has one job. Assemble them into a cell and find out whether it holds.
You have the parts list. Assemble a viable minimal cell and defend it against three failure modes.
sub: Then we will try to break it.
Then we will try to break it — three different ways.
Then it faces three stresses. Each one is survivable, but only by a specific part.
Each stress is diagnostic: it fails in a specific, findable way if a specific component is absent.

question: Which part could you leave out and still be alive?
Is there any one part you could leave out and still have a living cell?
Which single component is dispensable in a minimal cell?
Is minimal viability achievable with any proper subset of these components?
note: Commit to an answer, then test it by omission.
State it, then falsify it by construction.

trialsTitle: Now we try to break it
t: Put every part in its place. Then we test it.
Place every part in the job it does. Then the cell faces three stresses.
Assign each component to its function, then watch the assembled cell face three stresses.
Assemble the minimal set, then observe which stresses it survives and which it does not.

label: Keeps things out
Decides what gets in and out

Reads the message and builds protein

name: Poison in the water
Poison in the surroundings
pass: Steric exclusion at the membrane: the toxin never got in.
fail: With no boundary there is no selectivity, and the toxin entered freely.

name: No food for a while
Starvation
pass: It burned its reserves and held on.
Stored substrate was oxidised to ATP fast enough to cover demand.
fail: Nothing could turn the reserves into energy.
Without oxidative capacity, reserves are inert: ATP demand goes unmet within seconds.

name: Something broke and needed replacing
Damage requiring repair
pass: It read the instructions and built a new one.
Transcript out, ribosome reads it, replacement protein synthesised — powered by ATP.
fail: It had no way to make a replacement.
Repair needs the instruction, the machinery to read it, and the energy to run it. Missing any one and the damage is permanent.

win: It survived everything. That is a working cell.
It survived all three. Every part earned its place — and you can see exactly which stress each one answered.
lose: Look at which test it failed, put that part in, and try again.
Read which trial failed: it names the missing component. Place it and the same stress becomes survivable.

t: Four parts. Take any one away and it stops being alive.
Four parts, four jobs, and no spares. Take one away and the whole thing stops.
A cell is not a bag of parts. Each component depends on the others: remove one and functions that seemed unrelated fail with it.
Viability is a property of the assembly, not of any component. That interdependence is the reason no one has yet built a cell from scratch.
sub: That is what being alive means: all the parts working at once.
That is why a cell is like a city and not like a brick — every part needs the others.
This is why the minimal genome question is hard: 'essential' is only definable relative to a whole system.
Minimal-genome work has driven the count below 500 genes and still finds roughly a fifth of them of unknown function. The system resists reduction.

t: Doctors work out what is wrong by finding which part stopped working.
Diagnosis is largely this exercise in reverse: from what is failing, work out which part broke.
Clinical reasoning runs this backwards — a pattern of failures implies a specific broken component, which is why symptoms cluster the way they do.
Mitochondrial, lysosomal and ribosomopathic diseases each present with a characteristic tissue pattern precisely because the failure is componentwise and tissues differ in demand.

q: Why did taking one part away break more than one thing?
Why did removing a single part cause several different failures?
Why do component failures produce effects that look unrelated?
Why is the failure signature of a missing component broader than its stated function?
options: Because the parts all depend on each other
why: Repair needed the instructions AND the builder AND the energy. Take away any one and repair stops, even though only one part is missing.
Most functions use several parts at once. Repair needs the instructions, the builder and the energy — so losing the power plant breaks repair as well as everything obviously energy-related.

Functions are composite. Repair depends on transcript, ribosome and ATP simultaneously, so a mitochondrial defect presents as a repair defect too. Interdependence is why symptom clusters look surprising.
Because functions are multiply dependent. The observable phenotype of a lesion is the union of every composite process that requires it, not the component's nominal role.
